South Asia Snapshot - September 7, 2026

Defense Alliances, Key Summits, and Climate Risks

Getty Images

Dear Readers,South Asia is officially a region that does not take time off, even in August. The month brought a packed agenda: significant defense pacts, key summits, and attempts to make sense of what comes next in the U.S.-Iran space. The region also experienced another climate catastrophe as flash floods devastated Nepal. Let’s take a look at what happened last month and why it matters.Pakistan and the Evolving Middle EastAugust opened with the signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan, an effort to build collective deterrence in an increasingly volatile and conflict-prone region.The pact stipulates, in language reminiscent of NATO’s Article 5, that “any armed attack against any one of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” A similar provision was included in the bilateral Saudi-Pakistan mutual defense agreement signed last year.  Having emerged against the backdrop of ongoing U.S.-Iran tensions, the agreement does not identify a specific adversary and remains open to other countries with shared interests, potentially leaving the door open for Qatar and Egypt to join in the future. Interestingly, Bangladesh was reportedly also invited, adding another dimension to what is becoming a more consequential South Asia–Middle East security nexus.The pact quickly drew international attention. President Trump welcomed the development, writing on X that he was “very happy” to see countries building their own meaningful defense capabilities. Iran has also indicated that it is not concerned that the pact is intended to exert pressure on Tehran.There are still few details in the public domain about the pact’s full provisions. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan clarified that a country under attack would need to request assistance and specify the required support. He also said the agreement would strengthen the three countries’ joint capacity through military training, intelligence sharing, and greater interoperability.Why It Matters: The pact, officially now the Mecca Defense Alliance, highlights the gradual emergence of a more networked Middle Eastern security order. Regional middle powers, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan are pooling complementary strengths—Saudi financial weight, Turkish defense capabilities and NATO experience, and Pakistani military prowess—to create more room for independent regional action without solely relying on external guarantees.The pact was put to an early test almost immediately after its signing as Saudi-Houthi tensions flared. There was no activation of the agreement, but the episode offered an early indication of how the arrangement might function in practice. Last week saw the alliance’s first Strategic Political and Defense Committee meeting as the three countries move quickly to institutionalize their cooperation under a Saudi Arabia-based secretariat with a Pakistan secretary-general at the helm for the initial three-year period.For the United States, on one hand, the pact is a sign of Washington’s diminishing influence in the Middle East. On the other, it aligns closely with the Trump administration’s longstanding demand that allies and partners shoulder more of the burden for their own defense. For India, the agreement will be watched closely. The development could further propel India’s already growing ties with the UAE and Israel as it seeks to deepen its own strategic partnerships across the Middle East.For Pakistan, the pact adds another layer to its growing global relevance. Islamabad has also signed a defense pact with Kuwait, just weeks after the latter ratified the agreement. At the same time, Pakistan continues to seek diplomatic space between the United States and Iran amid escalating tensions, continuing its role as the key mediator. Field Marshal Asim Munir traveled to Tehran once again last month to meet with key Iranian officials. Munir also reportedly spoke with President Trump before the Iran visit.Nevertheless, Pakistan’s diplomatic leverage has its limits. The widening trust deficit between Washington and Tehran makes an already difficult path to mediation even more arduous. For Islamabad, the challenge will be sustaining this diplomatic momentum without overextending its hand.The SCO and India’s Multi-AlignmentThe Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) marked its 25th anniversary in Kyrgyzstan against rising U.S.-Iran tensions, renewed sanctions threats, and complex intra-group dynamics. The Bishkek Declaration called for deeper cooperation on AI, trade, connectivity, counterterrorism, and energy, while notably opposing “unilateral coercive measures” and signaling support for member Iran without directly naming the United States. Why It Matters: The SCO is becoming a useful platform for political signaling and strategic leverage amid growing global fragmentation, even as members remain divided on explicitly anti-Western positioning. China’s influence within the grouping is nevertheless increasingly evident, with Xi’s four-point proposal at the summit reflecting Beijing’s strategic priorities. The upcoming BRICS summit in India will offer further signals of how these competing interests will shape interest-based groupings and the international order, developments Washington will watch closely.Some of the more consequential diplomacy unfolded on the sidelines. Prime Minister Modi’s meeting with Putin was notable, with Modi stressing that “we must move from endless war to the end of war.” He also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, their first meeting since the start of the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict, highlighting New Delhi’s effort to preserve its multi-alignment and maintain diplomatic space while engaging across competing geopolitical camps.Modi also arrived from Uzbekistan, where India elevated bilateral ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, discussed expanding trade, and secured uranium supplies. The moves reflect New Delhi’s active hedging and broader push to deepen engagement with Central Asia as the region gains strategic and economic importance.Nepal FloodsOn August 26, disaster struck along the Nepal-Tibet border as a glacial collapse triggered a deadly flood wave that swept downstream into Nepal. The devastating episode claimed more than 1,000 lives, with many still missing in both Nepal and Tibet as rescue operations continue. Entire settlements and critical infrastructure were washed away, making it one of the worst disasters Nepal has experienced in recent decades. Nepal’s Prime Minister Balen Shah has called for global efforts to address climate risks, while the finance minister has warned that the country could need up to $5 billion to rebuild, a staggering burden for a nation with limited fiscal space and new leadership.Why It Matters: The disaster is yet another wake-up call to the growing climate vulnerability of the Himalayan region. Rapid warming, melting glaciers, and the region’s seismic geography are creating interconnected hazards.That complexity makes monitoring, early warning, and risk assessment far more difficult and underscores the need for hyperlocal assessments and preparedness.The international response was swift. The United States announced $3.6 million in assistance, while China sent emergency relief supplies to Nepal to support rescue and relief operations. India was also quick to provide emergency aid and humanitarian assistance.At the same time, the crisis exposes the limitations of existing international climate-finance and disaster-response mechanisms. They remain inadequate to match the scale and frequency of increasingly severe climate events in vulnerable regions that are disproportionately impacted. It also emphasizes the urgent need for regional coordination, including timely data sharing, joint early-warning systems, coordinated disaster response, and capacity-building, given the inherently transboundary nature of Himalayan climate risks.Stay Tuned! The summit season isn’t over yet. We will be back soon with UNGA coverage and the BRICS Summit in New Delhi. Keep following along.Warmly,Farwa Aamer
